full_text_en:
Supreme People's Court

Notice of the Supreme People's Court on Issuing the Fifth Batch of Guiding Cases

Fa [2013] No. 241

To: The High People's Courts of all provinces, autonomous regions, and municipalities directly under the Central Government; the Military Court of the People's Liberation Army; and the Production and Construction Corps Branch of the High People's Court of the Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region:

Upon deliberation and decision by the Judicial Committee of the Supreme People's Court, the six cases including the dispute over a sales contract between Zhang Li and Beijing Heli Huatong Automotive Service Co., Ltd. (Guiding Cases No. 17-22) are hereby issued as the fifth batch of Guiding Cases for reference in the adjudication of similar cases.

November 8, 2013

Guiding Case No. 17

Zhang Li v. Beijing Heli Huatong Automotive Service Co., Ltd. — dispute over a sales contract

(Deliberated and adopted by the Judicial Committee of the Supreme People's Court, issued on November 8, 2013)

Keywords: Civil; sales contract; fraud; household automobile

Ruling Gist

1. Where an automobile is purchased for the purpose of household consumption needs and a dispute over fraud arises, the matter may be handled in accordance with the Law of the People's Republic of China on the Protection of Consumer Rights and Interests.

2. Where an automobile seller promises to sell a new car that has not been used or repaired to a consumer, and the consumer discovers after purchase that the automobile has been used or repaired, if the seller cannot prove that it has fulfilled the obligation of disclosure and obtained the consumer's approval, it constitutes sales fraud. If the consumer requests the seller to compensate for losses in accordance with the Law on the Protection of Consumer Rights and Interests, the people's court shall support such a claim.

Relevant Legal Provisions

Article 2 and Paragraph 1 of Article 55 of the Law of the People's Republic of China on the Protection of Consumer Rights and Interests (this paragraph was amended on October 25, 2013; previously it was Article 49).

Basic Facts

On February 28, 2007, the plaintiff, Zhang Li, purchased a Shanghai GM Chevrolet Epica sedan from the defendant, Beijing Heli Huatong Automotive Service Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Heli Huatong Company), for RMB 138,000. The parties signed an Automobile Sales Contract. Article 7 of the contract stipulated: "... The seller guarantees that the vehicle purchased by the buyer is a new car and has undergone necessary inspection and cleaning before delivery. The odometer reading of the vehicle is 18 kilometers and it meets all specifications and indicators listed in the delivery documents provided by the seller to the buyer..." On the day the contract was signed, Zhang Li paid the purchase price of RMB 138,000 to Heli Huatong Company, as well as vehicle purchase tax of RMB 12,400, a one-stop service fee of RMB 500, and insurance premiums of RMB 6,060. On the same day, Heli Huatong Company delivered a Chevrolet Epica sedan to Zhang Li, who completed the motor vehicle registration procedures for the car. On May 13, 2007, when Zhang Li sent the vehicle to Heli Huatong Company for maintenance, she discovered that the car had been repaired on January 17, 2007.

During the trial, Heli Huatong Company stated that the vehicle purchased by Zhang Li had indeed been scratched during transportation and had been repaired on January 17, 2007. The repair items included: spray painting of the right front fender, spray painting of the right front door, spray painting of the right rear fender, sheet metal work on the right front door, sheet metal work on the right rear fender, and sheet metal work on the right front fender. The bottom sill clips, fuel filler door, and front fender light assembly were replaced during the repair. The person who sent the vehicle for repair was a business representative of the company. Heli Huatong Company claimed that it had clearly informed Zhang Li of the vehicle's repair history at the time of sale and had accordingly offered a substantial discount. It stated that the list price of the vehicle should have been RMB 151,900, but after negotiation, the actual selling price was RMB 138,000, and some decorations were also provided as a gift. To prove these facts, Heli Huatong Company provided the vehicle maintenance records and a vehicle handover and acceptance form dated February 28, 2007, bearing Zhang Li's signature. In the remarks column of the vehicle handover and acceptance form, it was noted: "Plus 1/4 tank of oil, this car has sheet metal and paint repair on the right side, sold at agreed price." Heli Huatong Company stated that the form was retained by the company, and Zhang Li did not have a copy. Regarding the two pieces of evidence provided by Heli Huatong Company, Zhang Li stated that she had no objection to the vehicle maintenance records and acknowledged that the signature on the vehicle handover and acceptance form was hers, but she claimed that Heli Huatong Company had not informed her of the vehicle's repair history at the time of sale and that when she signed the form, the remarks column did not contain the words "this car has sheet metal and paint repair on the right side, sold at agreed price."

Judgment

The Chaoyang District People's Court of Beijing Municipality rendered a civil judgment (2007) Chao Min Chu Zi No. 18230 on October 2007: 1. Rescind the Automobile Sales Contract signed between Zhang Li and Heli Huatong Company on February 28, 2007; 2. Zhang Li shall return the purchased Chevrolet Epica sedan to Heli Huatong Company within seven days after the judgment takes effect; 3. Heli Huatong Company shall refund RMB 124,200 of the purchase price to Zhang Li within seven days after the judgment takes effect; 4. Heli Huatong Company shall compensate Zhang Li for the purchase tax of RMB 12,400, the service fee of RMB 500, and the insurance premiums of RMB 6,060 within seven days after the judgment takes effect; 5. Heli Huatong Company shall pay double the purchase price of RMB 138,000 as punitive damages to Zhang Li within seven days after the judgment takes effect; 6. Dismiss Zhang Li's other claims. After the judgment was pronounced, Heli Huatong Company appealed. The Beijing Second Intermediate People's Court rendered a civil judgment (2008) Er Zhong Min Zhong Zi No. 00453 on March 13, 2008: Dismiss the appeal and affirm the original judgment.

Reasoning

The effective judgment of the court held that: The plaintiff, Zhang Li, purchased the automobile for personal and household living needs. The defendant, Heli Huatong Company, provided no evidence that Zhang Li purchased the car for business or other non-household consumption purposes. Therefore, Zhang Li's purchase of the automobile constituted a household consumption need and was subject to the Law of the People's Republic of China on the Protection of Consumer Rights and Interests.

According to the terms of the Automobile Sales Contract signed by both parties, the vehicle delivered by Heli Huatong Company to Zhang Li should have been a new car with no repair history. It was a fact acknowledged by both parties that the vehicle sold had actually undergone repairs before delivery. Thus, the focus of the dispute in this case was whether Heli Huatong Company had fulfilled its disclosure obligation in advance.

A reduction in or discount on the vehicle's selling price, along with free car decorations, are common sales strategies used by sellers and are the result of negotiations between the parties. This cannot be inferred as Heli Huatong Company having disclosed the vehicle's defects to Zhang Li and then offering a discount or price reduction. Regarding the vehicle handover and acceptance form bearing Zhang Li's signature submitted by Heli Huatong Company, since it was retained unilaterally by Heli Huatong Company, the content in the remarks column was written by different employees of the company, and Zhang Li did not acknowledge it, this form was insufficient to prove that Zhang Li was aware of the vehicle's prior repair history. Therefore, Heli Huatong Company's defense that it had fulfilled its obligation to disclose the defects to Zhang Li was not accepted. It was determined that Heli Huatong Company had concealed the vehicle's defects at the time of sale, constituting fraudulent conduct. Heli Huatong Company was ordered to accept the return of the vehicle, refund the purchase price, and pay additional compensation for Zhang Li's losses.

Guiding Case No. 18

ZTE Corporation (Hangzhou) Co., Ltd. v. Wang Peng — dispute over a labor contract

(Deliberated and adopted by the Judicial Committee of the Supreme People's Court, issued on November 8, 2013)

Keywords: Civil; labor contract; unilateral termination

Ruling Gist

A worker being ranked at the lowest level in an employer's performance appraisal is not equivalent to being "incompetent for the job" and does not meet the statutory conditions for the employer to unilaterally terminate the labor contract. The employer cannot unilaterally terminate the labor contract on this basis.

Relevant Legal Provisions

Articles 39 and 40 of the Labor Contract Law of the People's Republic of China

Basic Facts

In July 2005, the defendant, Wang Peng, began working for the plaintiff, ZTE Corporation (Hangzhou) Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as ZTE). The labor contract stipulated that Wang Peng would be engaged in sales work, with a base monthly salary of RMB 3,840. The company's Employee Performance Management Measures provided that: Employee performance appraisals for semi-annual and annual periods were classified into four grades: S, A, C1, and C2, representing excellent, good, values non-conformity, and performance needs improvement, respectively. The proportions for S, A, and C (C1, C2) grades were 20%, 70%, and 10%, respectively. In principle, those found incompetent for their jobs would be rated as C2 in the appraisal. Wang Peng originally worked in sales in the company's distribution department. After January 2009, due to the dissolution of the distribution department and other reasons, he was transferred to a sales position in the East China region. Wang Peng's appraisal results for the second half of 2008, the first half of 2009, and the second half of 2010 were all C2. ZTE considered that Wang Peng was incompetent for his job and, after being transferred to another position, remained incompetent. Accordingly, ZTE terminated the labor contract after paying a portion of the economic compensation.

On July 27, 2011, Wang Peng applied for labor arbitration. On October 8, 2011, the arbitration commission issued an award: ZTE was to pay Wang Peng the balance of compensation for the illegal termination of the labor contract, totaling RMB 36,596.28. ZTE believed it had not illegally terminated the labor contract and therefore filed a lawsuit with the court on November 1, 2011, requesting a judgment that it was not obligated to pay the balance of compensation for the termination of the labor contract.

Judgment

The Binjiang District People's Court of Hangzhou City, Zhejiang Province, rendered a civil judgment (2011) Hang Bin Min Chu Zi No. 885 on December 6, 2011: The plaintiff, ZTE Corporation (Hangzhou) Co., Ltd., shall pay the defendant, Wang Peng, the balance of compensation for the illegal termination of the labor contract in the amount of RMB 36,596.28 in a single lump sum within fifteen days after the effective date of this judgment. After the judgment was pronounced, neither party appealed, and the judgment became legally effective.

Reasoning

The effective judgment of the court held that: To protect the legitimate rights and interests of workers and to establish and develop harmonious and stable labor relations, the Labor Law of the People's Republic of China and the Labor Contract Law of the People's Republic of China clearly define the conditions under which an employer can unilaterally terminate a labor contract. The plaintiff, ZTE, terminated the labor contract on the grounds that the defendant, Wang Peng, was incompetent for his job and remained incompetent after being transferred to another position. ZTE bore the burden of proof for this claim. According to the Employee Performance Management Measures, "the proportion of C (C1, C2) assessment grades is 10%." Although Wang Peng had received a C2 assessment result, a C2 grade is not entirely equivalent to being "incompetent for the job." ZTE could not prove the worker's incompetence for the job based solely on this assessment result, which was subject to a predetermined grade proportion, and thus did not meet the statutory conditions for unilaterally terminating the labor contract. Although Wang Peng was transferred from the distribution department in January 2009, he was engaged in sales work both before and after the transfer. Moreover, the fundamental reason for Wang Peng's transfer was the dissolution of the distribution department. Therefore, it could not be proven that Wang Peng was transferred due to incompetence for the job. Consequently, ZTE's claim that Wang Peng was incompetent for his job and remained incompetent after the transfer was unsupported. The termination constituted an illegal dissolution of the labor contract, and ZTE was required to pay Wang Peng double the statutory economic compensation standard as compensation.

Guiding Case No. 19

Zhao Chunming, et al. v. Yantai Fushan District Automobile Transportation Company, Wei Deping, et al. — dispute over liability for a motor vehicle traffic accident

(Deliberated and adopted by the Judicial Committee of the Supreme People's Court, issued on November 8, 2013)

Keywords: Civil; liability for motor vehicle traffic accident; fake license plate; joint and several liability

Ruling Gist

Where a motor vehicle owner or manager lends its license plate to another person for use on a fake license plate vehicle, or, knowing that another person is using a fake license plate bearing its number, fails to stop such use, and the fake license plate vehicle is involved in a traffic accident causing damage to others, the motor vehicle owner or manager shall bear joint and several liability together with the owner or manager of the fake license plate vehicle.

Relevant Legal Provisions

Article 8 of the Tort Liability Law of the People's Republic of China

Article 16 of the Law of the People's Republic of China on Road Traffic Safety

Basic Facts

At approximately 5:30 a.m. on November 25, 2008, the defendant, Lin Zedong, while driving a truck bearing the fake license plate Lu F41703 on a section of the Tong-San Expressway, collided with a bus driven by the defendant, Zhou Yaping, traveling in the same direction. Both vehicles went off the road embankment, and the bus rolled over, causing the death of a passenger, Feng Yongju, on the spot. According to the determination of the traffic police department, the truck driver, Lin Zedong, bore primary responsibility, the bus driver, Zhou Yaping, bore secondary responsibility, and Feng Yongju bore no responsibility for the accident. The plaintiffs, Zhao Chunming, Zhao Moumou, Feng Moumou, and Hou Moumou, were the husband, son, father, and mother of the deceased, Feng Yongju, respectively.

The truck registered with the vehicle management department under the license plate Lu F41703 was not the accident-causing truck. The owner of the registered truck was the defendant, Yantai Fushan District Automobile Transportation Company (hereinafter referred to as Fushan Company), and its actual owner was the defendant, Wei Deping. This truck was insured with the defendant, Yongan Property Insurance Co., Ltd., Yantai Central Sub-branch (hereinafter referred to as Yongan Insurance Company), for compulsory motor vehicle third-party liability insurance.

The actual owner of the truck bearing the fake license plate Lu F41703 (the accident-causing truck) was the defendant, Wei Guanghui, and Lin Zedong was a driver employed by Wei Guanghui. According to vehicle management department registration records, the truck registered under license plate Lu F41703 had applied for replacement license plates and vehicle registration certificates on 15 occasions between April 26, 2004, and July 2, 2008, on the grounds of damage or loss. The application form for a replacement vehicle registration certificate submitted by Wei Guanghui on August 23, 2007, bore the seal of Fushan Company. After the incident, Fushan Company sent personnel to the traffic police department to handle related matters. During the trial, Wei Guanghui stated that Wei Deping was aware of the use of the fake license plate and had collected a fee for it. After the incident, Wei Guanghui even borrowed the insurance policy for the truck registered under Lu F41703 from Wei Deping to handle the accident, and the policy was still in Wei Guanghui's possession.

The registered owner of the bus involved in the accident was the defendant, Zhu Rongming. However, the bus had changed hands several times, and the actual owner at the time of the accident was Zhou Yaping. Zhu Rongming neither controlled the bus nor benefited from its operation. The defendant, Shanghai Tengfei Construction Engineering Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Tengfei Company), was Zhou Yaping's employer, but Zhou Yaping was not performing his duties at the time of the accident. The bus was insured with the defendant, People's Insurance Company of China, Shanghai Branch (hereinafter referred to as PICC Shanghai Branch), for compulsory motor vehicle third-party liability insurance.

Judgment

The Baoshan District People's Court of Shanghai Municipality rendered a civil judgment (2009) Bao Min Yi (Min) Chu Zi No. 1128 on May 18, 2010: 1. Defendants Wei Guanghui and Lin Zedong shall compensate the four plaintiffs for funeral expenses, moral damages, death compensation, transportation expenses, lost work expenses, accommodation expenses, dependent living expenses, and attorney fees totaling RMB 396,863; 2. Defendant Zhou Yaping shall compensate the four plaintiffs for funeral expenses, moral damages, death compensation, transportation expenses, lost work expenses, accommodation expenses, dependent living expenses, and attorney fees totaling RMB 170,084; 3. Defendants Fushan Company and Wei Deping shall bear joint and several liability for the compensation obligation under item 1 of the main text of this judgment; defendants Wei Guanghui, Lin Zedong, and Zhou Yaping shall bear reciprocal joint and several liability for the compensation obligations under items 1 and 2 of the main text of this judgment; 4. Dismiss the plaintiffs' other claims. After the judgment was pronounced, Wei Deping appealed. The Shanghai Second Intermediate People's Court rendered a civil judgment (2010) Hu Er Zhong Min Yi (Min) Zhong Zi No. 1353 on August 5, 2010: Dismiss the appeal and affirm the original judgment.

Reasoning

The effective judgment of the court held that: According to the determination of liability for this traffic accident, the accident-causing truck driver, Lin Zedong, bore primary responsibility. Wei Guanghui was the actual owner of the accident-causing truck and Lin Zedong's employer. Therefore, Wei Guanghui and Lin Zedong should jointly bear primary compensation liability for the losses resulting from this accident. The Lu F41703 truck insured by Yongan Insurance Company was not the actual accident-causing truck, and Yongan Insurance Company was unaware that the Lu F41703 license plate was being used on a fake license plate truck. Therefore, Yongan Insurance Company was not liable for compensation in this accident. According to the determination of liability for the traffic accident, the bus driver, Zhou Yaping, bore secondary responsibility for the accident and was also the actual owner of the bus. Therefore, Zhou Yaping should bear secondary compensation liability for the losses resulting from this accident. Although Zhu Rongming was the registered owner of the bus, the bus had changed hands several times, and Zhu Rongming neither controlled the bus nor benefited from its operation. Therefore, he was not liable for this accident. Although Zhou Yaping was employed by Tengfei Company, he was not performing his duties for Tengfei Company at the time of the accident. Therefore, Tengfei Company was also not liable in this case. As for PICC Shanghai Branch, which insured the bus, because the deceased, Feng Yongju, was an occupant of the bus, the compulsory motor vehicle third-party liability insurance was not applicable by law. Therefore, PICC Shanghai Branch was not liable in this case. Furthermore, although the proportion of liability to be borne by Wei Guanghui and Lin Zedong on one side, and Zhou Yaping on the other side, differed, the accident resulted from the joint tortious conduct of both sides. Therefore, Wei Guanghui and Lin Zedong were reciprocally jointly and severally liable for the proportionate liability of Zhou Yaping, and Zhou Yaping was reciprocally jointly and severally liable for the proportionate liability of Wei Guanghui and Lin Zedong.

The registered owner of the Lu F41703 truck, Fushan Company, and its actual owner, Wei Deping, knowing that Wei Guanghui and others were using a fake license plate bearing their vehicle's number and failing to stop it, and providing convenience, thereby conniving at the operation of the fake license plate truck on the road. The conduct of Fushan Company and Wei Deping constituted lending their vehicle license plate to others for use. This conduct violated the provisions of the Law of the People's Republic of China on Road Traffic Safety and other motor vehicle management laws. Lending a vehicle license plate to another person for use on a fake license plate will condone the operation on the road of motor vehicles that do not meet safety technical standards through the use of fake plates, increasing the danger of road traffic and endangering public safety. Where a fake license plate motor vehicle causes damage in a traffic accident, the person who lent the license plate also bears fault and should bear joint and several liability for the compensation liability of the accident-causing fake license plate vehicle owner. Therefore, Fushan Company and Wei Deping were to bear joint and several liability for the compensation liability share of Wei Guanghui and Lin Zedong.

Guiding Case No. 20

Shenzhen Siruiman Fine Chemical Co., Ltd. v. Shenzhen Kengzi Water Supply Co., Ltd. and Shenzhen Kangtailan Water Treatment Equipment Co., Ltd. — dispute over infringement of invention patent

(Deliberated and adopted by the Judicial Committee of the Supreme People's Court, issued on November 8, 2013)

Keywords: Civil; intellectual property; infringement of invention patent; provisional protection period; subsequent conduct

Ruling Gist

Where the manufacture, sale, or import of an alleged patent-infringing product during the provisional protection period (i.e., between the publication of the invention patent application and the grant of the patent right) is not prohibited by the Patent Law, the subsequent use, offering for sale, or sale of that product shall not be deemed as patent infringement, even without the permission of the patentee. However, the patentee may request, in accordance with the law, the payment of appropriate fees from the entity or individual that exploited the invention during the provisional protection period.

Relevant Legal Provisions

Articles 11, 13, and 69 of the Patent Law of the People's Republic of China

Shenzhen Siruiman Fine Chemical Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Siruiman Company) filed an invention patent application with the State Intellectual Property Office on January 19, 2006. The patent was published on July 19, 2006, and was granted and announced on January 21, 2009. The title of the granted invention was "Device for Preparing High-Purity Chlorine Dioxide," and the patentee was Siruiman Company. The most recent annual fee payment for this patent was made on November 28, 2008. On October 20, 2008, Shenzhen Kengzi Tap Water Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Kengzi Tap Water Company) and Shenzhen Kangtailan Water Treatment Equipment Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Kangtailan Company) entered into a "Purchase and Sale Contract." Under the contract, Kengzi Tap Water Company purchased one set of Kangtailan chlorine dioxide generator from Kangtailan Company at a price of RMB 260,000. Kangtailan Company had already requested the tax authority to issue a unified invoice for the above product sales proceeds on December 30, 2008. The said "Purchase and Sale Contract" stipulated that Kengzi Tap Water Company would pay the equipment amount to Kangtailan Company in installments, and Kangtailan Company would provide Kengzi Tap Water Company with technical support and after-sales services such as installation, commissioning, repair, and maintenance.

On March 16, 2009, Siruiman Company filed a lawsuit with the Shenzhen Intermediate People's Court of Guangdong Province, alleging: It owned the invention patent entitled "Device for Preparing High-Purity Chlorine Dioxide" (hereinafter referred to as the patent-in-suit). The chlorine dioxide production equipment manufactured and sold by Kangtailan Company and used by Kengzi Tap Water Company fell within the scope of protection of the patent-in-suit. It requested the court to order the two defendants to cease infringement and compensate for economic losses of RMB 300,000, and to bear litigation costs and other expenses. In this case, Siruiman Company did not raise a claim for payment of a reasonable royalty for the use of the invention during the provisional protection period of the patent. Even after the court of first instance had explained the matter, Siruiman Company insisted on its original claims.

Judgment

The Shenzhen Intermediate People's Court of Guangdong Province rendered a civil judgment (2009) Shen Zhong Fa Min San Chu Zi No. 94 on January 6, 2010, ordering: Kangtailan Company to cease the infringement; Kangtailan Company and Kengzi Tap Water Company to jointly and severally compensate Siruiman Company for economic losses of RMB 80,000. Both Kangtailan Company and Kengzi Tap Water Company appealed. The Guangdong High People's Court rendered a civil judgment (2010) Yue Gao Fa Min San Zhong Zi No. 444 on November 15, 2010, dismissing the appeal and affirming the original judgment. Kengzi Tap Water Company, dissatisfied with the second-instance judgment, applied to the Supreme People's Court for retrial. The Supreme People's Court rendered a civil judgment (2011) Min Ti Zi No. 259 on December 20, 2011, reversing the original first and second-instance judgments and dismissing Siruiman Company's claims.

Reasoning

The Supreme People's Court held: In this case, Siruiman Company did not raise a claim for payment of a reasonable royalty for the use of the invention during the provisional protection period of the patent. Therefore, the main focus of the dispute was whether Kengzi Tap Water Company's use, after the grant of the patent-in-suit, of the allegedly infringing patent product purchased from Kangtailan Company during the provisional protection period of the patent-in-suit constituted infringement of the patent-in-suit, and whether Kangtailan Company's provision of after-sales services to Kengzi Tap Water Company for the use of the allegedly infringing patent product after the grant of the patent-in-suit constituted infringement of the patent-in-suit.

The determination of patent infringement must comprehensively consider the relevant provisions of the Patent Law. Based on the timing of the allegedly infringing acts in this case, the Patent Law of the People's Republic of China as amended in 2000 should apply. Article 11, paragraph 1 of the Patent Law provides: "After the grant of a patent for invention or utility model, except as otherwise provided for in this Law, no entity or individual may, without the authorization of the patentee, exploit the patent, that is, may not, for production or business purposes, manufacture, use, offer to sell, sell, or import the patented product, or use the patented process and use, offer to sell, sell, or import the product directly obtained by the patented process." Article 13 provides: "After the publication of an application for a patent for invention, the applicant may require the entity or individual that exploits the invention to pay an appropriate fee." Article 62 provides: "The statute of limitations for litigation concerning patent infringement is two years, counted from the date on which the patentee or an interested party became aware or should have become aware of the infringing act. Where no appropriate fee has been paid for the use of an invention during the period between the publication of the patent application for invention and the grant of the patent right, the statute of limitations for the patentee to claim payment of the fee is two years, counted from the date on which the patentee became aware or should have become aware of the use of its invention by others. However, if the patentee became aware or should have become aware of such use before the date of grant of the patent right, the statute of limitations shall be counted from the date of grant of the patent right." Taking the above provisions into comprehensive consideration, the Patent Law provides that an applicant may require an entity or individual that exploits its invention during the period between the publication of the patent application for invention and the grant of the patent right (i.e., the provisional protection period of the patent) to pay an appropriate fee, i.e., enjoys the right to claim payment of a reasonable royalty for the use of the invention during the provisional protection period. However, it does not enjoy the right to demand cessation of the exploitation of the invention during the provisional protection period. Therefore, exploiting the relevant invention during the provisional protection period of a patent for invention is not an act prohibited by the Patent Law. In circumstances where the manufacture, sale, or import of the allegedly infringing patent product during the provisional protection period is not prohibited by the Patent Law, the subsequent acts of using, offering to sell, or selling such product should be permitted, even without the authorization of the patentee. That is, the patentee has no right to prohibit others from the subsequent use, offer to sell, or sale of the allegedly infringing patent product that was manufactured, sold, or imported during the provisional protection period. Of course, this does not negate the patentee's right, under Article 13 of the Patent Law, to exercise its right to claim an appropriate fee from the entity or individual that exploited its invention. For an allegedly infringing patent product manufactured, sold, or imported during the provisional protection period, where the seller or user provides a legal source, the seller or user shall not bear the responsibility to pay an appropriate fee.

Determining that the subsequent acts of using, offering to sell, or selling, after the grant of a patent for invention, products obtained from exploiting the invention during the provisional protection period do not constitute infringement is consistent with the legislative purpose of the Patent Law. On the one hand, the original design of the patent system is "disclosure in exchange for protection," and protection can only be sought after the grant of the patent. For a patent application for invention, exploiting the relevant invention before the publication date does not constitute infringement, and subsequent exploitation of products obtained from the exploitation of the invention before the publication date should also be permitted after the publication date; during the period between the publication date and the grant date, provisional protection is provided for the patent application for invention, and exploiting the relevant invention during this period is not prohibited by the Patent Law. Likewise, subsequent exploitation of products obtained from exploiting the invention during this period should also be permitted after this period ends. However, after obtaining the patent right, the applicant has the right to require the entity or individual that exploited its invention during the provisional protection period to pay an appropriate fee. Since the Patent Law does not prohibit the exploitation of an invention before the grant of a patent for invention, subsequent exploitation of products manufactured before the grant of the patent does not constitute infringement. Otherwise, it would contradict the legislative intent of the Patent Law by providing protection for technical solutions that have not yet been published or granted. On the other hand, the Patent Law provides for the right of prior use. Although it only provides that a prior user continuing to manufacture the same product or use the same process within the original scope does not constitute infringement, and does not specify whether subsequent exploitation of the same product manufactured or the product manufactured using the same process constitutes infringement, this does not mean that the lack of an explicit provision in the Patent Law leads to a determination that such subsequent exploitation constitutes infringement. Otherwise, the right of prior use provided for in the Patent Law would be meaningless.

In this case, Kangtailan Company's sale of the allegedly infringing patent product occurred during the provisional protection period of the patent-in-suit, an act not prohibited by the Patent Law. Under these circumstances, Kengzi Tap Water Company's subsequent use of the purchased allegedly infringing patent product should also be permitted. Therefore, Kengzi Tap Water Company's subsequent use does not infringe the patent-in-suit. Similarly, Kangtailan Company's provision of after-sales services to Kengzi Tap Water Company for the use of the allegedly infringing patent product after the grant of the patent-in-suit does not infringe the patent-in-suit.

Guiding Case No. 21

Inner Mongolia Qiushi Real Estate Development Co., Ltd. v. Hohhot People's Air Defense Office — administrative case concerning the collection of fees for civil air defense

(Discussed and adopted by the Judicial Committee of the Supreme People's Court, published on November 8, 2013)

Keywords: administration; administrative collection of civil air defense fees; air defense; basement; fee for alternative construction

Ruling Gist

Where a construction unit violates the Law of the People's Republic of China on Civil Air Defense and relevant regulations by failing to build an air defense basement that should be built, it constitutes an illegal act of failing to perform a statutory obligation. Where a construction unit should pay the fee for the alternative construction of a civil air defense basement in accordance with the law, the provisions on "exemption from various administrative charges such as urban infrastructure supporting fees" applicable to construction projects of indemnity housing such as low-rent housing and economically affordable housing shall not apply.

Related Laws

Article 22 and Article 48 of the Law of the People's Republic of China on Civil Air Defense

Basic Facts

On September 10, 2008, the defendant, Hohhot People's Air Defense Office (hereinafter referred to as Hohhot Air Defense Office), served a "Notice on Completing the Examination and Approval Procedures for 'Combined Construction' within a Time Limit" to the plaintiff, Inner Mongolia Qiushi Real Estate Development Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Qiushi Real Estate Company). The notice informed Qiushi Real Estate Company that its newly constructed economically affordable housing residential community project, "Qiushi First City," had not built a basement usable for wartime air defense simultaneously, in violation of Article 22 of the Law of the People's Republic of China on Civil Air Defense and Articles 45 and 47 of the "Regulations on the Construction and Management of Civil Air Defense Projects." Qiushi Real Estate Company was required to complete the "combined construction" procedures at Hohhot Air Defense Office before September 14 and submit relevant materials. On June 18, 2009, Hohhot Air Defense Office issued a "Decision on Collecting the Fee for Alternative Construction of Civil Air Defense Basement" (Hu Ren Fang Zheng Fei Zi No. 001) to Qiushi Real Estate Company, deciding to collect a "fee for the alternative construction of a civil air defense basement" of RMB 1,724,600 for the "Qiushi First City" project. Qiushi Real Estate Company had no objection to the fact that it should have built a civil air defense basement of 5,518 square meters for the "Qiushi First City" project but did not, and had no objection to the legality of the procedure by which Hohhot Air Defense Office made the fee-collection decision.

Judgment

The Xincheng District People's Court of Hohhot City, Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region, rendered an administrative judgment (2009) Xin Xing Chu Zi No. 26 on January 19, 2010, sustaining the "Decision on Collecting the Fee for Alternative Construction of Civil Air Defense Basement" (Hu Ren Fang Zheng Fei Zi No. 001) issued by Hohhot Air Defense Office. After the judgment was announced, Qiushi Real Estate Company appealed. The Hohhot Intermediate People's Court rendered an administrative judgment (2010) Hu Xing Zhong Zi No. 16 on April 20, 2010, dismissing the appeal and affirming the original judgment.

Reasoning

The court's effective judgment held: Article 16 of the State Council's "Several Opinions on Solving the Housing Difficulties of Urban Low-Income Families" provides: "All administrative charges such as urban infrastructure supporting fees and government funds shall be exempted for the construction of low-rent housing and economically affordable housing, shantytown renovation, and renovation of old residential areas." Article 8 of the "Measures for the Administration of Economically Affordable Housing" jointly issued by the Ministry of Construction and six other ministries provides: "Construction projects of economically affordable housing shall be exempted from various administrative charges such as urban infrastructure supporting fees and government funds." Although the above provisions on exemption from various administrative charges for construction projects of indemnity housing such as economically affordable housing do not explicitly specify their objects, from the legislative intent, the objects they refer to should be lawful construction activities. Article 22 of the Law on Civil Air Defense provides: "New civil buildings in cities shall, in accordance with relevant state regulations, build basements that can be used for wartime air defense." Article 48 of the "Regulations on the Construction and Management of Civil Air Defense Projects" provides: "For civil buildings that should, according to regulations, build air defense basements, if construction is not suitable due to geological, topographical, or other reasons, or if the required construction area is less than the ground floor area of the civil building, upon approval by the competent department of civil air defense, the basement may not be built, but the fee for alternative construction must be paid based on the cost required for the area of the air defense basement that should have been built, and the competent department of civil air defense shall arrange for nearby alternative construction." That is, only in circumstances where laws and regulations provide that building an air defense basement is not suitable can construction projects of indemnity housing such as economically affordable housing avoid building an air defense basement and be eligible for the relevant provisions exempting them from paying the fee for alternative construction of a civil air defense basement. The objects to which the provisions on exemption from paying the fee for alternative construction of a civil air defense basement apply should not include illegal construction activities; otherwise, the cost of illegal acts would be less than the cost of lawful acts, which would contravene the legislative purpose and be detrimental to safeguarding national defense security and the fundamental interests of the people. Since Qiushi Real Estate Company failed to build the air defense basement that it should have lawfully built, it committed an illegal act of failing to perform a statutory obligation and is not eligible for the preferential provisions on exemption from paying the fee for alternative construction of a civil air defense basement.

Guiding Case No. 22

Wei Yonggao and Chen Shouzhi v. People's Government of Lai'an County — case concerning the withdrawal of land use rights approval

(Discussed and adopted by the Judicial Committee of the Supreme People's Court, published on November 8, 2013)

Keywords: administrative litigation; scope of accepting cases; approval

Ruling Gist

An approval issued by a local people's government in response to a request for instructions from its subordinate administrative department is generally an internal administrative act and cannot be challenged by litigation. However, if the administrative department directly implements such approval, thereby producing actual effects on the rights and obligations of administrative counterparts, and the administrative counterparts, dissatisfied with the approval, initiate an administrative lawsuit, the people's court shall accept the case in accordance with the law.

Related Laws

Article 11 of the Administrative Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China

Basic Facts

On August 31, 2010, the Bureau of Land Resources and Housing Management of Lai'an County, Anhui Province, submitted a "Request for Instructions on Withdrawing the Right to Use State-Owned Land" to the People's Government of Lai'an County, requesting the withdrawal of the land use rights for certain parcels of land on Yongyang East Road and Tashan Middle Road in the county. On September 6, 2010, the People's Government of Lai'an County issued an "Approval on Agreeing to Withdraw the Right to Use State-Owned Land for Certain Parcels on Yongyang East Road and Tashan Middle Road." After receiving this approval, the Bureau of Land Resources and Housing Management of Lai'an County did not, in accordance with the law, prepare and serve a notice of withdrawal of land use rights on the original land use right holders; instead, it directly handed the matter over to the Land Reserve Center of Lai'an County for implementation. The houses of Wei Yonggao and Chen Shouzhi were located within the land area subject to the withdrawal of use rights. Dissatisfied with the approval of the People's Government of Lai'an County to withdraw the state-owned land use rights, they filed an application for administrative reconsideration. On September 20, 2011, the People's Government of Chuzhou City issued an "Administrative Reconsideration Decision," upholding the approval of the People's Government of Lai'an County. Still dissatisfied, Wei Yonggao and Chen Shouzhi initiated an administrative lawsuit, requesting the people's court to revoke the above approval of the People's Government of Lai'an County.

Judgment

The Chuzhou Intermediate People's Court rendered an administrative ruling (2011) Chu Xing Chu Zi No. 6 on December 23, 2011, dismissing the lawsuit filed by Wei Yonggao and Chen Shouzhi. Wei Yonggao and Chen Shouzhi appealed. The Anhui High People's Court rendered an administrative ruling (2012) Wan Xing Zhong Zi No. 14 on September 10, 2012: 1. Reversing the administrative ruling (2011) Chu Xing Chu Zi No. 6 of the Chuzhou Intermediate People's Court; 2. Ordering the Chuzhou Intermediate People's Court to continue the trial of this case.

Reasoning

The court's effective judgment held: According to the procedural provisions of the "Measures for the Administration of Land Reserve" and the "Measures of Anhui Province on the Reserve of State-Owned Land" concerning the reserve of state-owned land through withdrawal, after the people's government of Lai'an County issued the approval approving the plan to withdraw the state-owned land use rights, the competent administrative department for land and resources of Lai'an County should have served a notice of withdrawal of state-owned land use rights, which would have external legal effect, on the original land use right holders. The approval of the People's Government of Lai'an County was an internal administrative act, not served on the counterparts, and had not yet produced actual effects on the rights and obligations of the counterparts. Generally, it does not fall within the scope of accepting cases for administrative litigation. However, in this case, after the People's Government of Lai'an County issued the approval, the competent administrative department for land and resources of Lai'an County did not prepare and serve a legal instrument with external effect; instead, it directly handed the matter over to the Land Reserve Center of Lai'an County to implement the demolition, compensation, and resettlement activities based on that approval. This produced actual effects on the rights and obligations of the original land use right holders. Moreover, the original land use right holders became aware of the content of the approval by applying for government information disclosure and filed an administrative reconsideration against the approval. When the reconsideration authority made its reconsideration decision, it also informed the right to sue. The approval had been actually implemented and externalized into a specific administrative act with external legal effect. Therefore, an administrative lawsuit challenging this approval should be accepted by the people's court in accordance with the law.
